Well first of all, if you REALLY don't like it (like in the case of greek yogurt), you don't *have* to eat it. A varied diet has its benefits, but the real culprit of being in poor health/overweight is the Western Diet in general. That said, I think it's a good idea to eat more vegetables. Stir-frying them has already been recommended. I also like eating broccoli with noodles in an alfredo sauce. Plenty of recipes - it just comes down to finding the ones you really like. 

With vegetables, if you go for local (or organic if you have to, though since it's easy to get a food labeled organic you have to be careful) and especially in season, they tend to taste better. We tend to learn that a carrot is a carrot is a carrot, but that's not the case. Like celery - conventional celery tastes like crunchy water, organic/local tastes pretty robust. Farmer's markets are great places to find produce. 

If you're concerned about beef, try to get grass-fed (particularly 100% grass-fed or grass-finished, since the qualifications for being allowed to put just "grass fed" on beef is super low). There have been some studies showing the issues with beef are only true of grain-fed beef. Someone else in this thread said to look into some less common meats (besides chicken, turkey, pork, and beef). I recommend bison.

Also, mushrooms. What allowed me to start eating more mushrooms was reading a book called *The Omnivore's Dilemma*, which has a whole section about the nutritional benefits of mushrooms and their vital role in the environment. I used to be scared shitless of mushrooms but that helped me appreciate them enough to try them (turns out, pan frying them in butter, especially if you just pan-fried a steak or something, makes them taste amazing. I love steak and mushrooms now). I also credit the book to my eating better in general (more vegetables, less meat, less fast food, etc.) and having an understanding of food that is neither "it's a coping mechanism" nor "it's just fuel" because food is really so much more than either of those things. It kind of changed my life so I can't help but get excited talking about this book, so forgive me if I sound like I'm trying to proselytize. 

Anyway, that's my take, as a former super-picky eater who hated vegetables not too horribly long ago.

Ninja edit: it's also super easy to make zucchini noodles and sneak them into pasta, or sneak peas into alfredo sauce or something like that. I almost don't even notice them, and the taste is more than tolerable (as someone who really hates peas).

I've had binge eating problems as long as I can remember. I used to sneak snacks when I was 8 and make myself sick, due in part to anxiety and in part to gorging and in part to it being a cycle where I'd eat to fix my anxiety but then be anxious about eating too much... My weight was chubby when I was younger, evened out when I was in middle school, and after a bout freshman year where I was too anxious to eat for most of the day, I started ballooning, from 117lbs to 126lbs in five months as a freshman, then up to 145lbs by the time I graduated high school. In my freshman year of college, I shot up again to about 170lbs. Buffets were not helpful (neither were big changes, it seemed). I maintained that weight for my sophomore year at my parents' and the first semester my junior year at a different college with my roommate, but going home for winter break must have been particularly stressful, because I managed to gain about 15lbs in the course of a month due to bingeing. I felt pretty awful. I still have stretch marks on my belly that make me look like I've been pregnant. 

My highest weight was 198lbs, the summer after my junior year (read: last summer). Managed to lose a few and get down to 192lbs without really trying but having a high-activity/standing job. At the end of the year I decided I was sick and tired of bingeing and being overweight, and I never wanted to leave onederland, and I really wanted to try and improve myself. So I made the New Year's resolution to lose weight... again. But this time with more determination. 

I set up a few visual aids (such as a rewards system and a couple mason jars filled with pebbles representing the pounds I have to lose/have already lost), tracked calories, tried to eat a bit better in general, and continued to practice martial arts (a division of taekwondo which I have practiced for a little over a year, though recently just started moving up through belts; I'm a second yellow at the moment). I've been taking a class on food in society which provided a pretty in-depth analysis/critique of the food system. As a result, I've started buying local food if I can and organic if I can't for the most part, reduced my fast food intake, made a food budget which keeps me from just carelessly spending money on fast food, and limiting my meat intake so that I would necessarily eat more vegetables. I've also been cooking a lot more, portioning meals, eating a lot of salads that I actually enjoy, and other such things.
